issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 355-94-1 Estate Tax: Nonresident
text:
Ruling 355-94-1
Issued: July 12, 1994
Effective: July 12, 1994
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Estate
Tax Act to the following facts:
X died in 1993 while a resident of another state. X and X's spouse owned property in
several states including New Mexico. X through X's will and estate planning
anticipated no taxes to New Mexico because of the federal unified credit.
Subsequent to filing an estate return for X in one of the other states (not the state in
which X was domiciled), a decision of that state's supreme court affecting the value
of X's property in that state may mean that X's estate now has a federal estate tax
liability.
X's representative asks if X will owe any New Mexico estate tax on income arising from the
property located out-of-state?
Section 7-7-2 NMSA 1978 defines "net estate" to mean "taxable estate" as defined in Section
2051 of the United States Internal Revenue Code.
Section 7-7-4 NMSA 1978 prescribes how estates of nonresidents who have property in
New Mexico are to be taxed. It states in part:
“A. Tax in an amount computed as provided in this section is imposed on
the transfer of the net estate located in New Mexico of every nonresident...
B. The tax shall be computed by multiplying the federal credit by a
fraction, the numerator of which is the value of the property located in New Mexico
and the denominator of which is the value of the decedent's gross estate.” (Emphasis
added)
...
D. The transfer of the property of a nonresident is exempt from the tax imposed
by this section to the extent that the property of residents is exempt from taxation under the
laws of the state in which the nonresident is domiciled.”
If the New Mexico estate tax applies at all to the value of a decedent's property in New
Mexico, Section 7-7-4(B) NMSA 1978 requires the estate tax be calculated for nonresidents as a
percentage of the federal Section 2011 credit. This is to avoid the fruitless debate over which asset or
assets triggered the federal tax liability. It is as equally valid to claim that the New Mexico assets are
to be added on top of the sum of the assets in the other states to determine which portion of the estate
bears the burden of the federal tax as it is to claim that the estate assets in another state are added to
New Mexico assets and that, therefore, only those out-of-state assets bear the federal tax. All assets
of a federally-taxable estate wherever located contribute proportionately to the size of the gross
estate and to the taxable portion.
X will have a New Mexico estate tax liability if the value of X's estate is such that a federal
Section 2011 credit arises unless the provisions of Subsection D of Section 7-7-4 NMSA 1978
apply.
If Subsection D does not apply, the New Mexico liability equals the maximum amount of the

federal Section 2011 credit for X's estate times a fraction, the numerator of which is the value of X's
New Mexico property and the denominator of which is the gross value of X's estate.
If the state in which X was domiciled exempts the transfer of the property of nonresidents
from that state's estate, inheritance or equivalent tax, then the transfer of X's New Mexico property
would be exempt from New Mexico estate tax pursuant to Subsection D of Section 7-7-4 NMSA
1978.
